items.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996
items.q: if you check out Shakespeare... he’s telling his daughter he says, “pity the poor man who has no music within his soul”

ctx.x: Well that was at the time. And it just showed you that, like I said how powerful music is. Because if you check out Shakespeare, if I can remember what it was, Shakespeare, talking to the daughter in “The Merchant of Venice,” and you’ll find a part in there, I’m trying to figure what chapter it is, but he’s telling his daughter he says, “pity the poor man who has no music within his soul, for this person is guilty of treason.” And he goes on to elaborate about the person who has no music within him. And you check…

hundred years whenever archeologists, wherever they go and they find they discover ruins from the most primitive tribes to the most sophisticated and advanced, they always find some form of art, dance and music, which means that the human being has always entertained themselves, from the very beginning.
